# Tidal Locking and Its Profound Influence on Planetary Climates

Tidal locking occurs when a planet's orbital period matches its rotational period, causing one hemisphere to face its star permanently. This phenomenon, common among planets orbiting red dwarf stars, creates some of the most extreme and fascinating climates in the universe.

The most obvious consequence is the dramatic temperature contrast between hemispheres. The dayside, bathed in perpetual starlight, can reach scorching temperatures of hundreds of degrees, while the nightside plunges to frigid extremes where atmospheres may even freeze out. On a tidally locked planet without sufficient atmosphere, the temperature difference between the two hemispheres could exceed several hundred degrees.

Atmospheric circulation becomes the planet's lifeline. On Earth, sunlight drives winds and weather patterns; on a tidally locked world, the temperature differential creates powerful, persistent winds flowing from dayside to nightside at the terminator—the twilight zone between hemispheres. These winds transport heat from the day side to the night side, potentially moderating temperatures enough to maintain liquid water on the dayside. Climate models suggest that a sufficiently dense atmosphere, perhaps a few bars of pressure, could keep surface temperatures habitable across much of the planet.
